title: Undercurrents: resource dependence strategies across the adaptive cycle in a critical raw material-dependent supply network
authors: Felix Kissi Dankyira; Iryna Malacina; Anni-Kaisa Kähkönen
affiliations: LUT University Business School, , ,
abstract: Purpose The study aims to examine how firms in a supply network (SN) dependent on critical raw materials (CRMs) adapt to environmental uncertainty arising from contemporary geopolitical tensions. To address this aim, we draw on the theoretical lenses of adaptive cycles of the panarchy theory and resource dependence theory. Design/methodology/approach We employ a sequence-structuring theoretical elaboration approach, treating adaptation as an evolving process, to investigate adaptive responses to geopolitical tensions within CRM-dependent SN. We use primary interview data from 19 informants, comprising 3 industrial experts and 16 senior executives within firms embedded in a Nordic SN dependent on CRMs. These data are complemented with SN- and firm-level secondary data. Interview data were analysed abductively using thematic analysis, while SN data were analysed using a theoretically derived set of network structural measures as complementary contextual evidence. Findings We find that across the phases of the adaptive cycle, firms systematically reconfigure their strategies. During conservation and release, firms prioritise negotiating with the environment and avoiding dependencies to preserve continuity and restore short-term adaptability under high uncertainty. In contrast, during reorganisation and exploitation, firms rely on absorbing the environment and creating the environment to redesign dependency structures and support longer-term strategic renewal and growth. Under conditions of high dependency, firms tend to normalise geopolitical risk rather than respond adaptively to it. Originality/value This study advances empirically grounded, process-oriented research on how responses unfold across SN adaptive cycle phases during geopolitical tensions.

title: Issue Information
Computational Creativity in the AI Era: A Research Agenda for Information Systems
authors: Min Ding; Ram Gopal; Ulrike Schultze; D. J. Wu
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802; The University of Warwick, Coventry CV4 7AL, United Kingdom; University of Groningen, 9712 CP Groningen, Netherlands; Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332
abstract: This editorial presents computational creativity as a durable research program for Information Systems. Defining creativity as a structured, instrumentable, and improvable process of search, recombination, evaluation, and realization, we conceptualize computational creativity as being concerned with computational systems that model, simulate, enact, or augment the creative behavior of human creators. The five articles in this Special Issue show that the promise of computational systems—in particular, generative AI—lies in configuring human and machine agency so that creative work produces ideas and artifacts that are deemed creative—that is, novel and useful—while also safeguarding the generative, effortful, accountable, and socially meaningful nature of creativity. We translate these findings into an IS research agenda focused on process instrumentation, diversity-preserving design, agency-sensitive governance, organizational capability building for human-AI creative systems, and responsible computational creativity. The core challenge is to engineer the practices of computational creativity without forfeiting either the novelty or usefulness of the output, or human agency.

title: The first bear raid and squeeze: Isaac Le Maire and the Dutch East India Company
authors: Oscar Gelderblom; Abe de Jong; Joost Jonker
affiliations: Faculty of Arts, Department of History University of Antwerp Antwerp Belgium; Faculty of Economics and Business, Department of Economics, Econometrics, and Finance University of Groningen Groningen the Netherlands; Monash Business School, Department of Banking and Finance Monash University Melbourne Australia; Faculty of Humanities, Department of History University of Amsterdam Amsterdam the Netherlands
abstract: Abstract In 1609, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) faced a bear raid by a syndicate of short sellers led by Isaac Le Maire, a former director. We reconstruct the forward trade between 1607 and 1611, the actions taken by the syndicate members, and the responses to these actions by the company. We argue that the bear syndicate members aimed for financial gain from share price declines, while their leader, Le Maire, participated for strategic reasons, that is, breaking up the VOC monopoly. We also show that the government refused to intervene at that time. The raid ended with a squeeze executed by an opposing syndicate, bankrupting several forward traders and blocking Le Maire's plans. We characterize the bear raid and squeeze as a crucial episode in the more general tug‐of‐war between company directors aiming to turn the VOC into an instrument of the state and a diverse group of opposing investors.

title: Coloniality of care: Indigenous autonomy and the structuring of contemporary health regimes in Chile
authors: Dana Brablec
affiliations: University of Amsterdam, Netherlands
abstract: This article analyses intercultural health in Chile as a contested institutional regime through which colonial relations are reorganised rather than dismantled. Drawing on long-term, multi-sited ethnographic research conducted between 2016 and 2025, and informed by sociological approaches to governance, coloniality and the politics of recognition, it examines how Mapuche-Indigenous actors engage with state-led intercultural health programmes and how these arrangements structure relations of knowledge, authority and care. The analysis suggests that while institutionalised interculturality has seemingly reduced overt discrimination and expanded access to services, it has also subordinated Indigenous knowledge within bureaucratic and biomedical frameworks. At the same time, the Makewe Intercultural Hospital illustrates how interculturality can be reworked as an Indigenous-led project of institutional autonomy grounded in territorial governance, collective organisation and epistemic plurality. Although materially constrained and exceptional, Makewe illuminates the conditions under which alternative regimes of care can emerge within, yet in tension with, state health systems.

title: Beyond stereotypes: Examining the social backgrounds and life trajectories of women in sex work
authors: Stefan B. Andrade; Theresa D. Henriksen
affiliations: The Danish Center for Social Science Research, Copenhagen, Denmark
abstract: The question of who engages in sex work continues to attract attention. While recent research emphasises the heterogeneity of people who sell sex, little is known about how sex workers’ social backgrounds and life trajectories compare with those of their non-sex-worker peers. Applying a life-course perspective, we combine police records and social service registers with administrative data from Statistics Denmark to analyse the social backgrounds and life trajectories of 2478 female sex workers. Using latent class models, we assess social problems across childhood, adolescence and adulthood. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity, with most sex workers experiencing few problems while a small subgroup face elevated risks of mental health issues, crime, victimisation, substance misuse and homelessness. Analyses show that those with the most complex problems often come from disadvantaged families. Comparisons with two control groups highlight both similarities in and differences between the life trajectories of sex workers and other women.

title: Employment and Community: Socioeconomic Cooperation and Its Breakdown
authors: Daron Acemoglu; Alexander Wolitzky
affiliations: MIT ,
abstract: Abstract We model the interplay of employment relations and community-based interactions among workers and managers. Employment relations can be either tough (where workers are monitored intensively and obtain few rents, and managers do not provide informal favors for workers) or soft (where there is less monitoring, more worker rents, and more workplace favor exchange). Both workers and managers also exert effort in providing community public goods. The threat of losing access to public goods can motivate managers to keep employment soft; conversely, the threat of losing future employment or future workers’ trust can motivate workers and managers to provide effort in the community. Corporate tax cuts; improved worker monitoring; automation, outsourcing, and offshoring; declines in the minimum wage; and opportunities for residential segregation or for privatizing community-provided services can make both workers and managers worse-off by undermining soft employment relations and community cooperation.

title: The Family Job Hunt: The Influence of Family Member Active Job Search Behavior on Family–Work Conflict
authors: Michael Halinski; Jennifer A. Harrison
affiliations: Toronto Metropolitan University Ted Rogers School of Management Toronto Ontario Canada; Normandie Business School Le Havre France
abstract: ABSTRACT Existing research shows that family members may draw on work and personal resources to support job seekers. This research, however, explores the reverse: how the behaviors of job‐seeking family members may impact non‐job‐seekers' ability to manage work and life demands. Using the sustainable career ecosystem perspective and conservation of resources theory, we hypothesize that job search interdependence moderates the relationship between family member active job search behavior and non‐job‐seeker family–work conflict, and non‐job‐seeker work identity further amplifies these crossover effects. Study 1 employs a two‐wave, dyadic field study ( n 1 = 178 undergraduate child job seekers and their employed parents), whereas Study 2 employs a scenario‐based experiment ( n 2 = 483) involving a spouse job seeker and a non‐job‐seeking partner. Findings from both studies provide partial support for the moderation of job search interdependence in our model, as the pattern of findings shows an asymmetry by the type of job‐seeking family member (i.e., child versus spouse). In Study 2, the hypothesized three‐way interaction with work identity was not supported. Exploratory follow‐up analyses, however, indicated that the two‐way interaction emerged among non‐job‐seekers high in work identity but not among those low in work identity. These findings underscore the importance of family context for job searches and offer insights into effective work‐family strategies.

title: Who Are You Hanging Out With? The Conditional Importance of Investment Managers’ Personal Reputation in the Formation of Venture Capital Syndication Ties
authors: Massimo G. Colombo; Annalisa Croce; Elisa Ughetto
affiliations: Politecnico di Milano; Politecnico di Torino
abstract: Abstract We examine how the two dimensions of VC managers' personal reputation, that is, ‘being known’ and ‘being known for quality’, jointly influence the formation of initial syndication ties. We propose that VC managers follow a two‐stage cognitive process. In the first stage, the ‘being known for quality’ dimension – a reflection of their abilities‐must enter their ‘consideration set’. The ‘being known’ dimension is crucial to draw attention to potential candidates. In the second stage, lead VC managers evaluate the signal conveyed by the ‘being known for quality’ dimension of prospective partners' reputation. The ‘being known’ dimension is also important at this stage, as it allows for a more accurate assessment of what is otherwise a noisy signal. We test our hypotheses on a pairwise dataset of 1686 realized and 14,395 counterfactual initial syndication ties between VC managers. We find that lead VC managers are more likely to form initial syndication ties with VC managers with similar reputations. This effect is stronger if they share a previous common employer, have a similar industrial or geographic investment focus, or work at VC firms that have previously syndicated one or more investments with each other or with the same VC firm.

title: Freeriding and Rebellion: An Investigation of Open Source Vendor Relicensing and Member Hard Forking Events
authors: Dawn Foster; Matt Germonprez
affiliations: Board Member, CHAOSS London UK; Mutual of Omaha Distinguished Chair of Information Science & Technology, Professor of Information Systems and Quantitative Analysis, College of Information Science & Technology University of Nebraska Omaha Omaha Nebraska USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Open source engagement is an ongoing effort in which members continuously interact with evolving project dynamics. Engagement extends beyond writing code or setting policy; it is a shared practice of understanding, negotiating, and adapting to the social and technical structures that define a project. As members continually evaluate their project engagement, collective action threats may arise that impact the overall functioning and sustainability of a project. In our research, we investigate collective action threats and governance practices in relation to a recent trend of vendor defined licence changes that result in project members creating hard forks. Drawing on a netnographic analysis of three cases, Elasticsearch → OpenSearch, Terraform → OpenTofu, and Redis → Valkey, we develop theoretical and practical insights into what collective action threats and governance practices are present, their relationships, and who is involved in them within open source projects that experience relicensing and related hard fork events. Our research provides theoretical and practical implications that show how freeriding accusations become the justification for unilateral, non‐incremental adaptation to a project's boundary regulation and how these governance changes are tied to rebellion as project members reposition themselves within shifting open source landscapes and realign their future open source project engagements.
